draft.title: Coming home from war
card: When WWII ended, hundreds of thousands of Australian service personnel returned home. Many had physical injuries, such as lost limbs, or illnesses picked up in the field or as prisoners.

Many also carried lasting trauma. Memories of battle, captivity and lost mates could bring nightmares, anxiety and difficulty settling into family and work life. At the time, little was understood about this, and many people kept it to themselves.
The government offered help to returned personnel, such as pensions, medical care, job training and land for soldier settlers, who were given farms to start a new life.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander veterans had served alongside other Australians, but they were often left out of this help. Many were refused land or other support when they came home.
draft.remember: Coming home meant injury and trauma for many, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander veterans were often left out of the help offered.

a.q: Which of these was a common challenge for Australian personnel returning from WWII?
opts: Lasting trauma and physical injuries from service
Having no one willing to offer them any support
Being forced to return to their old jobs at once
Being unable to apply for any government help
a.why: Many returned with injuries and trauma that stayed with them long after the war. Support such as pensions, medical care and land did exist, so it is wrong to say there was no help at all.
a.clue: Think about what the war left in their bodies and minds.

b.q: Jack, an Aboriginal man from northern NSW, served in the army through WWII. After the war he applied for a farm under the soldier settler scheme but was turned down. What does his case show?
opts: Aboriginal veterans were often left out of offered help
Soldier settler land was only for injured veterans
Aboriginal people had not been allowed to serve in the army
The government gave land to no veterans after the war
b.why: Jack served like other soldiers, yet he was refused help that other returned personnel could receive. This shows Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander veterans were often left out. The scheme did give land to many other veterans, so it was not closed to everyone.
b.clue: Jack served like others, but did he get the same help?

a.best: Lasting trauma and physical injuries from service

b.best: Aboriginal veterans were often left out of offered help
